items.title: ‘No bank is too big to fail’: Inside the Deutsche Bank leaks
items.summary: Josy Joseph, the Indian author and journalist who obtained the Inside Deutsche Bank leak with South African investigative journalist Khadija Sharife, says the series shows a bank that made more money serving the corrupt than ordinary customers. In conversation with Nikita Saxena, he explains how whistleblower data reached him through a veteran lawyer, and why he chose to share custody with Sharife rather than run the project himself. The investigation was coordinated by Barracuda Media in South Africa, with technical support from the Data and Research Center (DARC) in Germany. Rather than publish the stories themselves, Joseph and Sharife passed the data on to newsrooms around the world (51 partners in 45 countries, over 250 journalists involved), especially the Global South. In his view, most global investigations are Western and hierarchical, with stories written mainly for readers in Europe and the US, while many of the victims of financial crime live in Asia, Africa and Latin America. items.title: Take the writ to the district court: An alternative to regional Supreme Court benches
items.summary: On November 4, Tamil Nadu Chief Minister C Joseph Vijay wrote to the Prime Minister seeking a Supreme Court Bench in Chennai, because access under Article 32 has become practically difficult for those far from Delhi. Six days later, Union Minister of State for Law and Justice Arjun Ram Meghwal said that evening courts, sitting beyond regular hours, would be piloted in Delhi, Bihar and Andhra Pradesh. A provision of the Constitution joins them and Parliament has left it unused for 76 years. The central question is whether the Chief Minister's objective can be met without the consent of the Supreme Court. The demand for a Bench is well supported, with the Law Commission's 95th, 125th and 229th Reports and the Parliamentary Standing Committee's 2nd, 6th, 15th, 20th and 133rd Reports among those favouring regional benches. Its difficulty is constitutional. Under Article 130, the Chief Justice of India appoints other places of sitting with the approval of the President. The Full Court rejected the proposal in August 2007 and reiterated its position in February 2010. A 2016 reference to a Constitution Bench is still pending. The Prime Minister cannot grant what the letter seeks. Article

items.summary: The Supreme Court will set up a permanent committee to address issues concerning the rights of disabled persons, Chief Justice of India (CJI) Surya Kant announced on Wednesday. CJI Kant also directed the Supreme Court Legal Services Committee to constitute panels of young lawyers and sign language interpreters to assist advocates with disabilities during proceedings before the Court. The announcements were made during a meeting between CJI Kant and Heba Hagrass , the United Nations' Special Rapporteur on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities at the Supreme Court. Lawyers with disabilities and representatives of civil society also attended the meeting. During the interaction, CJI Kant observed that ensuring the rights of disabled persons is a constitutional obligation and that equality is a fundamental principle of the Constitution. He stressed the need to identify gaps in the implementation of laws and government schemes to ensure that persons with disabilities could exercise their rights in practice. items.title: Foreigners accused of visa overstay can't be kept in detention centres after getting bail: Delhi High Court
items.summary: The Delhi High Court has ruled that foreign nationals accused of overstaying their visas cannot be directed to remain in detention centres as a condition for being granted bail. A Bench of Justices Navin Chawla and Arun Bhardwaj said that imposing such a condition would defeat the very purpose of granting bail. It added that foreign nationals accused of violating immigration laws are entitled to be considered for bail in the same manner as other criminal accused. “A direction imposing a condition wherein the foreign national is restricted to a detention centre would frustrate the very order of bail and hence, cannot be imposed. Such a power can be exercised by the Central Government by an order under Section 3(2)(g) of the 1946 Act [Foreigners Act], or under Paragraph 8 of the Immigration and Foreigners Order, 2025,” the Court said. However, it clarified that granting bail does not legalise a foreign national's continued stay in India or operate as a substitute for a valid visa. items.title: Opinion: A fair umpire cannot fix India's tilted electoral playing field
items.summary: The country is arguing about its umpire. As this is written, the Chief Election Commissioner (CEC) is facing petitions in the Supreme Court and demands for his resignation. Fair umpiring matters, and it must be secured. But even a perfect umpire cannot fix the rules of the game. On a tilted pitch, the most honest umpire in the world will only preside fairly over an unfair match. I belong to the generation that let the pitch tilt. We complained at dinner tables and voted for the same symbols. The people we elected grew richer, their criminal cases grew heavier, and we learned to call it normal. The young have stopped calling it normal. When some of them were dismissed as cockroaches, they turned the insult into a movement that reached millions within days, on almost no money. I am proud of them. Only the young, it seems, still have the courage and the energy to ask uncomfortable questions of those in power. So I have written down the questions I believe go to the root, as a letter I hope they will make their own: to their elders, to those in power, and to our courts. The questions are theirs to ask. In the span of a month, the Thiruvananthapuram Municipal Corporation, ruled by the Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP), filed a case against organisers of a protest gathering and denied permission for another musical performance. The protest, held in October, in which actor and activist Prakash Raj participated, demanded the removal of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar, echoing the youth movement in Delhi. Voices were being raised across the country against alleged irregularities in the Special Intensive Revision of electoral rolls conducted by the Election Commission, that excluded crores of valid voters. In Thiruvananthapuram, nine organisers of the protest, called Collective for Democracy, were charged for holding the gathering without prior permission. items.title: Sonbhadra-Singrauli: The land that gives us light, and the people poisoned with its ash
items.summary: Sonbhadra-Singrauli, on the Uttar Pradesh–Madhya Pradesh border, is one of India’s largest coal mining and thermal power regions. Its mines and power plants supply electricity to homes and industries across the country. While the coal here lights up millions of homes across India, the people living on top of it say they are paying with their health. Residents describe a side of that story that rarely reaches the national debate, from its polluted air to its contaminated water and degraded soil. Dust and emissions from mining and power plants hang over the region, and the improper disposal of fly ash has raised serious concerns about its rivers, reservoirs and groundwater. Scientific studies have documented fluoride, arsenic, mercury and lead in the region, and fluorosis has been reported in several areas. Locals say livestock have died after drinking water contaminated with fly ash, and that farming and livelihoods are suffering. With few healthcare facilities nearby, many villagers have to travel far for treatment.
